Each member of the team wrote and reviewed a part of this report, prepared research, requirements or design material, or built the mapping prototype; Appendix B records each contribution and its reviewer.

After a disaster, Government, Police, Emergency Medical Services and Fire agencies need a shared and current picture of damaged buildings, people who may need help, dangerous hazards and passable roads. Existing research and operational systems address these needs separately and rarely show how uncertain their outputs are. This report proposes RescueVision, a multi-agency platform designed to turn drone and satellite imagery into one shared incident map. Its six proposed features are before-and-after building damage assessment with an indicative restoration cost, 2D and 3D mapping with vehicle-specific rescue routes, detection of partly visible people from the air, person tracking with assistance cases, compound hazard alerts such as floodwater near live power lines, and approved reports that agencies can share. Every AI result is designed to keep its model version and to remain a candidate until a person confirms it. The report reviews the relevant literature, specifies 167 requirements and ten use cases, and presents an architecture, database and interface design traced to those requirements. A preliminary prototype shows dated satellite imagery of one earthquake-affected area in a common 2D view. No model accuracy or system performance has yet been measured; training, evaluation and user testing are planned for Project II.

RescueVision is a proposed disaster-response support platform for authorized Government, Police, Emergency Medical Services (EMS) and Fire agencies. It combines the presentation of available damage-assessment information with two-dimensional and three-dimensional area views, person-related assistance records, reported hazards, and response guidance. Through a website and mobile application, the project aims to help users understand an affected area, coordinate assistance, and maintain response-status information while retaining human responsibility for decisions.

Understanding disaster impacts and preparing for effective response are central concerns in disaster risk reduction. The Sendai Framework for Disaster Risk Reduction 2015-2030 identifies understanding disaster risk and strengthening preparedness for effective response among its priorities [1]. This context motivates the investigation of systems that help emergency organizations interpret and share relevant information.

Remote sensing offers one source of information about the physical effects of a disaster. Gupta et al. introduce xBD, a dataset containing pre-disaster and post-disaster satellite imagery, building annotations, and damage labels for research into change detection and building damage assessment [2]. This supports the investigation of image-based assessment as an input to situational awareness. It does not establish the accuracy or effectiveness of RescueVision, which requires its own evaluation.

The proposed RescueVision scenario also involves information that imagery alone cannot establish: people awaiting assistance, reported hazards, changing street conditions, and the status of a response. The motivation is to place these information types in a coherent spatial and case-based context. A user should be able to understand what a record represents, where it applies, and whether its information is current or requires confirmation.

Responsible handling of this information is part of the project motivation. The United Nations Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs (OCHA) describes data responsibility as the safe, ethical, and effective management of personal and non-personal data in humanitarian action, and notes that disclosure of sensitive data may cause harm [3]. RescueVision therefore treats access to person-related information and the interpretation of uncertain observations as design concerns from the beginning.

The purpose of this chapter, which forms the introduction of the Software Requirements Specification (SRS) in this report, is to define the problem, intended audience, intended use, scope, terminology, and constraints of RescueVision. It establishes a common foundation for the system description, detailed requirements, and design presented in the subsequent report sections.

The document supports communication among the project team, supervisor, assessors, and relevant stakeholders. Its objectives and boundaries provide a basis for deciding which capabilities belong to the proposal and for checking that later requirements and design decisions describe the same system. The success criteria identify observable outcomes to be used when planning verification.

RescueVision is intended to support the review of a disaster-affected area by authorized users of the participating agencies. The website is envisaged as an environment for overview and coordination, while the mobile application supports relevant field interactions. Detailed user privileges are specified in the system-description and requirements sections.

A typical proposed use begins when incident-related information becomes available. This may include imagery used for damage assessment and separately supplied records concerning people, hazards, or response activities. An authorized user examines the area, selects a relevant record, reviews the information and its limitations, and records or coordinates the next action. Subsequent updates maintain the status of the assistance case.

Two-dimensional and three-dimensional views provide alternative spatial presentations where suitable data exist. Person tracking means following available person-related location or status updates within an authorized workflow. It does not establish continuous observation or automatic identification of people. Responder location and the location of a person requiring assistance are separate record types and must not be confused.

Route guidance is intended to help users interpret available movement options using relevant road and hazard information. The user remains responsible for assessing its suitability. A route is not a guarantee of current accessibility or safety. Similarly, image-derived damage information does not establish building occupancy, injury, or structural safety.

For the academic project, these activities are to be demonstrated through controlled scenarios and genuine preliminary evidence appropriate to the implementation stage. A demonstration does not establish readiness for operational emergency deployment.

RescueVision addresses the problem of presenting different types of disaster-related information in a form that supports a shared understanding of the affected area. In the proposed scenario, damage observations, assistance needs, hazard reports, and response updates may originate from different sources and may refer to different times. Users must determine how these records relate geographically and which information is suitable for a decision.

Fragmented information can create specific difficulties in this scenario. A recorded assistance need may lack a verified location; an otherwise relevant street may have a newly reported obstruction; and a responder may not know whether another organization is already handling a case. The project investigates how spatial presentation and structured case updates can make these relationships visible. These are the problems defining the proposed use scenario, rather than claims that every emergency organization follows the same procedures.

The central project question is how to combine available assessment information and response records while preserving their source, update status, and uncertainty. The intended contribution is a coherent workflow for review and coordination. Demonstrating reduced response time or improved rescue outcomes would require a separate operational evaluation.

The proposed platform connects an assessment component with a response-support environment. Suitable before-and-after imagery can provide a basis for building-related damage predictions and visual summaries. These analytical outputs are presented alongside separately sourced person-related records, reported hazards, and response information. Their common spatial context helps the user examine relationships without treating one information type as proof of another.

The website and mobile application are intended to support the progression from viewing an incident area to reviewing a case, coordinating an action, and updating its status. Detailed technology choices and model architectures are addressed in later sections; this chapter defines their intended role and boundaries.

The project aim is to support situational awareness and assistance coordination through an understandable presentation of available disaster-related information. Table 1-2 expresses the objectives to which detailed requirements and verification activities should be linked.

Functional acceptance does not by itself establish model quality. Damage assessment must also be evaluated on a specified held-out dataset, with the split, labels, metrics, and results reported. Suitable measures may include intersection over union for segmentation and per-class precision, recall, and F1 for damage classification. Section 3.2.4 proposes numerical performance and quality targets; they must be confirmed before final acceptance testing, using the agreed dataset, hardware, and intended use. No accuracy or speed result is claimed in this chapter.

This chapter reviews research and operational systems relevant to the proposed RescueVision platform. It is organised around six questions that follow the platform’s features: how disaster information is presented, how affected areas are understood in 2D and 3D, how damage cost is estimated, how people who need assistance are found and followed, how hazards affect movement, and how organisations coordinate a response. Each theme compares several sources, notes where they agree and differ, and ends with what the findings mean for RescueVision. Capabilities that RescueVision proposes are described as aims to be tested, not as demonstrated advantages.

Sources were found in IEEE Xplore, the ACM Digital Library, MDPI, Springer, Nature Scientific Data, arXiv and Google Scholar, and in the official documentation of operational systems. A source was included when it met one of three conditions: it was a peer-reviewed study of a technique the platform depends on, a public dataset the project uses or plans to use, or an official description of a comparable system. Each entry was checked against its publisher, DOI or official page before it was accepted. Appendix D records the search terms, the date of each search, the sources selected and the reason for selection, together with the team’s ranked list of candidate papers.

The project configuration names several models but has not yet produced trained results; the planned experiments are still pending. This chapter therefore reports what the source studies measured on their own benchmarks and states separately what still has to be measured on the project’s data.
The literature agrees that responders need information that is fast, map-based and honest about its accuracy. It agrees less on how one display can support shared understanding across teams.

Endsley’s model of situation awareness separates perceiving the elements of a situation, understanding what they mean and projecting what happens next [6]. It identifies attention and working memory as the limits on what an operator can absorb, so a display that lists raw detections leaves the hardest work, interpretation, to a user under stress. Wolbers and Boersma observed Dutch command teams building a common operational picture during exercises [7]. They concluded that the picture is better understood as a process of collective sensemaking than as a finished information product. The Sendai Framework also places understanding disaster risk first among its priorities [1].

Operational mapping services show how damage information is delivered in practice. Voigt et al. describe how the German Aerospace Center produced rapid satellite maps after the 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami and the 2005 Pakistan earthquake, using imagery obtained through the International Charter Space and Major Disasters [8]. The Copernicus Emergency Management Service formalises this into product types: a first estimate, a delineation of the affected extent and a grading of damage, each delivered as print-ready maps and as vector data [9]. These services establish a fixed damage legend, dated products and machine-readable layers as normal practice.

Presentation can also mislead. Kerle compared the satellite damage maps produced after the 2006 Yogyakarta earthquake with a ground survey [10]. Detailed maps underestimated the damage and missed large areas, and grid-based maps understated how widespread it was; sparse imagery and cloud cover limited both. Kerle and Hoffman argue that collaborative damage mapping must be designed around the user’s cognitive tasks rather than assuming that maps are read as intended [11]. SensePlace2 linked a map, a timeline and a text view of geolocated messages to support crisis situation awareness, but its evaluation involved eight participants, so it shows feasibility more than proven benefit [12].

The sources agree that the map is the shared view and that speed matters. They differ on whether a better product [8], [9] or a better process between people [7], [11] matters most. None of the operational products reviewed shows a confidence value for each building, although Kerle’s comparison shows that authoritative-looking maps can be wrong. For RescueVision, this supports dated layers, a fixed damage legend and exportable vector data, with model confidence and review status shown for every item. Whether that helps responders has to be tested with users.

Deep learning on paired before-and-after imagery is now the standard research approach to building damage mapping. Drone imagery and 3D reconstruction add detail that satellites miss. The main open problem is whether a model trained on one event works on the next.

Dell’Acqua and Gamba’s survey of earthquake damage mapping separates estimating where damage is from estimating how severe it is, and compares the strengths and weaknesses of optical and radar data [13]. The xBD dataset turned damage mapping into a shared benchmark. It pairs pre-event and post-event satellite images with building outlines and a four-level damage scale, and its final version contains 850,736 building annotations over 45,362 km² [2]. RescueVision’s main pipeline is designed around xBD.

Fully convolutional networks (FCNs) showed how to train a network to produce a class for every pixel [14]. U-Net added a decoder with skip connections that recover the detail lost as features are downsampled, which matters for building outlines [15]. Residual connections made deeper encoders trainable [16], and EfficientNet scales depth, width and image resolution together [17]. For change detection, Daudt et al. showed that Siamese fully convolutional networks, which pass both dates through matching branches, detect change accurately and run at least 500 times faster than earlier related methods [18]. Weber and Kané reported that how the xBD task is framed, including fusing both dates inside the network, mattered as much as the choice of architecture; their approach ranked among the top xView2 results [19].

The Transformer replaced recurrence with attention [20]. SegFormer applies a hierarchical Transformer encoder and a light decoder to segmentation [21]. DINOv3 learns image features without labels and adds Gram anchoring to keep pixel-level features stable during long training; its authors release versions pretrained on satellite imagery [22]. Benchmark scores do not guarantee field performance. Nex et al. tested a state-of-the-art convolutional network under operational conditions, with little or no training on the new site and under time limits, and showed that accuracy does not transfer automatically to a new event [24]. Drone datasets help when no pre-event image exists. FloodNet provides high-resolution drone images from Hurricane Harvey with pixel labels for flooded buildings and roads [25], and RescueNet provides 4,494 drone images from Hurricane Michael labelled in ten classes, including four building-damage levels and separate road-clear and road-blocked classes [26]. Each covers a single hurricane, so transfer to earthquakes or other regions is not established.

Three-dimensional data adds evidence that a top-down view hides. Vetrivel et al. combined convolutional features with 3D point cloud features from oblique aerial images; accuracy rose from about 91% to about 94%, and the gain on unseen sites reached 7 percentage points [27]. Fernandez Galarreta et al. used a drone point cloud to find structural collapse and oblique images to grade façades and roofs, as support for an analyst rather than a replacement [28]. Map position also has limits. Turner et al. reported 65–120 cm absolute error for drone mosaics georeferenced from camera positions alone and about 10–15 cm with ground control points [29], and the OpenDroneMap documentation warns that drone GPS alone is typically accurate to 2–6 m [30].

The sources agree that before-and-after comparison is stronger than single-image analysis when both images exist, and that 3D adds evidence of collapse. The open problems are transfer between events, the ambiguity between neighbouring damage levels and map position error. For RescueVision, this supports keeping both a before/after path and a post-event-only path, labelling which one produced each grade, reporting results on held-out events, and measuring map position error rather than assuming it.

Feature F1 adds an indicative restoration cost to each damage grade. The established reference for this kind of estimate is the FEMA Hazus methodology [31]. Hazus estimates direct building loss by combining the probability of each structural damage state (slight, moderate, extensive and complete) with a repair cost expressed as a ratio of the replacement cost for the building’s occupancy class. The method is designed for planning-level estimates over many buildings, not for valuing a single property.

Two limits follow for RescueVision. First, the xBD grades are visual categories, not the engineering damage states that Hazus uses, so any mapping between them is an assumption that must be stated. Second, Hazus replacement costs describe United States building stock; the unit costs and repair ratios for another region have to be collected locally. Kerle’s finding that remote-sensing damage maps can understate damage [10] also means that a cost total inherits any error in the grades beneath it.

For RescueVision, a cost range per building, with its assumptions visible and editable, follows the Hazus approach while avoiding false precision. The estimate is for prioritisation and planning; it is not an engineering survey or an insurance valuation.
IDENTIFYING AND FOLLOWING PEOPLE WHO NEED ASSISTANCE

Research finds people in need through two channels: what people report themselves, and what sensors observe. Each channel finds people the other misses, and neither finds people who are both silent and hidden.

Okolloh describes how Ushahidi was built during Kenya’s 2007–08 election crisis so that citizens could report incidents by SMS and the web and see them on a shared map [32]. Imran et al. survey methods for processing social media in emergencies and identify three persistent problems: information overload, judging which messages are credible, and prioritising message types such as requests for help [33]. Self-reporting scales to many people but reaches only those with a working phone and network.

Unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs) can survey an affected area and relay communication for survivors [34]. Detecting people from the air is harder than in ground-level photographs because people are small, seen from above and often partly hidden. Sambolek and Ivasic-Kos built the SARD dataset of 1,981 drone images of people simulating exhausted or injured hikers and compared Faster R-CNN, YOLOv4, RetinaNet and Cascade R-CNN; they chose YOLOv4 and tested its robustness to fog, snow and motion blur [36]. Božić-Štulić et al. reported a detection rate of 88.9% at a precision of 34.8% on the HERIDAL search-and-rescue images [40], which shows that a high detection rate can come with many false alarms. Lygouras et al. ran a person detector on board a rescue drone to locate swimmers and release a flotation device [41]. VisDrone is a general drone benchmark recorded over Chinese cities, not a disaster dataset, but it shows that detecting and tracking small people from the air remains difficult [42]. ByteTrack improves tracking by also associating low-confidence detections, which reduces broken tracks when people are partly hidden [43].

A detection must also be placed on the map. Liu et al. show that single-image geolocation is sensitive to errors in drone position, camera angle and target height, and that combining several views improves accuracy [44]; the GPS tag of a photograph gives the camera’s position, not the person’s. People buried under rubble cannot be seen by RGB cameras at all. The MURMUR radar from MIT Lincoln Laboratory detects breathing through concrete and debris [45], but its public description is a project page, so its field accuracy is not established by the source.

The sources agree that no single channel finds everyone and that aerial detections produce false alarms. For RescueVision, this supports treating every detection as a candidate for human review, attaching a position uncertainty in metres to each one, and bringing citizen requests, responder reports and drone detections into one list of assistance cases. Detection of people under rubble is outside the scope of the aerial feature.
Road blockage, flooding and shortest-path routing are each well studied. Research rarely joins them, and few systems treat the interaction between hazards as a hazard in its own right.

Rastiveis et al. compared a pre-event road map with post-earthquake satellite images of Port-au-Prince and labelled roads as blocked or open; all 60 roads in a 1.2 × 0.8 km test area were labelled correctly, a small test that depends on an up-to-date road map [46]. RescueNet labels road-clear and road-blocked pixels directly in drone images [26], and FloodNet labels flooded roads [25]. Yin et al. coupled a flood model with the road network of central Shanghai and found that road disruption depends on rainfall pattern, drainage and terrain, and grows non-linearly with flood severity [47].

Routing research supplies the algorithms. Dijkstra’s algorithm finds shortest paths in a weighted graph [48], A* speeds the search with a distance estimate [49], and D* Lite repairs an existing route when part of the map changes instead of planning again from scratch [50]. Yuan and Wang modelled emergency routing in which road speed falls as a disaster spreads [51]. pgRouting provides these algorithms inside a spatial database [52].

Hazards also interact. Gill and Malamud reviewed 21 natural hazards and identified 90 interactions in which one hazard triggers or increases the likelihood of another [53]. Kappes et al. explain why analysing several hazards together is harder than analysing each alone, because both the hazard levels and the vulnerability to each process interact [54]. Public guidance warns that floodwater can contain downed power lines and advises against entering or driving through water where lines are down [55]. This combination of floodwater and live electrical infrastructure is the scenario behind the proposed Electrified Water alert.

The sources agree that blocked and flooded roads should be treated as costs or exclusions in a road network and that conditions change after an image is taken. They differ in where road state comes from: maps and imagery, learned segmentation or flood models. None of the routing studies reviewed carries the uncertainty of a detected road state into the route, and none of the mapping systems reviewed raises an alert when two hazards combine. For RescueVision, this supports routing per vehicle with closed and too-deep segments excluded, re-planning when a road closes, treating an unknown power state as energised, and reporting how often a blocked road is wrongly marked safe.

Coordination research finds that failures come more from organisations not sharing understanding than from missing technology. Operational systems exist for imagery, volunteers and rescue teams, but each covers one part of the work.

Comfort analysed the response to Hurricane Katrina through cognition, communication, coordination and control, and argued that coordination broke down when agencies did not share an understanding of the risk [56]. Bharosa et al. combined a literature review with observations and a survey from multi-agency exercises and grouped the obstacles to information sharing at community, agency and individual levels [57]. The National Incident Management System gives responding organisations common terminology and an incident command structure [58]. Humanitarian data-responsibility guidance adds that sharing sensitive data can cause harm, so access must follow purpose and role [3].

Operational mechanisms cover different parts of the work. The International Charter Space and Major Disasters lets an authorised national agency request satellite imagery during the immediate response [59]. The HOT Tasking Manager splits a mapping area into small tasks for volunteers, and experienced mappers validate each task [60]. The INSARAG Guidelines set international standards for urban search-and-rescue teams, including a coordination cell and a shared marking system for searched structures [61]. Sahana is an open-source disaster management system developed in Sri Lanka and described with a deployment case study [62].

The sources agree that coordination depends on shared standards and shared understanding, not only on software. For RescueVision, this supports one shared incident that a lead agency opens and other agencies join, common role names across agencies, access limited to agencies whose participation is active, and outputs that can be exported to partners. Whether this improves coordination is a hypothesis that would need a tabletop exercise or a field trial to test.

The intended users of RescueVision are local and national agencies (Government, Police, Emergency Medical Services and Fire) that fly their own drones or receive satellite imagery and need to act on it together. The international services above deliver satellite maps to national authorities within hours [9], [59], but the sources reviewed do not describe an open platform that turns that imagery into shared damage, people, hazard and route records for several local agencies at once. A market assessment of adopters, prices and procurement was outside the evidence collected for this report. One practical constraint applies to any use beyond research: the Maxar Open Data imagery used in the prototype is licensed for non-commercial use [64].

The reviewed research and systems treat damage mapping, finding people, movement planning and coordination separately, and they rarely show users how uncertain each output is. No source reviewed evaluates one platform in which several agencies share a single incident and every AI result keeps its provenance until a person confirms it. Four specific gaps support this statement.

First, damage models are not shown to transfer to new events: accuracy drops under operational conditions [24], the drone datasets each cover a single hurricane [25], [26], and authoritative-looking maps have understated real damage [10]. Second, provenance and uncertainty are rarely visible: none of the operational products in Table 2-3 shows confidence or review status per item, and detection position error is seldom reported with detection accuracy [44]. Third, people-finding channels are not joined: self-reports [33], [32], aerial detections [36] and rescue procedures [61] sit in separate systems, and the hand-over between agencies is a known obstacle [57]. Fourth, compound hazards are recognised in hazard research [53], [54] but not acted on in the routing and mapping systems reviewed, which do not close roads or warn teams when floodwater meets live power lines.

RescueVision responds with one shared multi-agency incident, AI results that keep their model version and remain candidates until a person confirms them, assistance cases that join drone, responder and citizen sources, and a rule-based compound hazard alert that closes roads and re-plans routes. Section 3.2 turns these responses into requirements, Section 3.3 designs them, and Chapter 4 reports the limited evidence produced so far. Whether they close the gaps can only be shown by the evaluations described in Chapter 5.

This section describes the proposed RescueVision platform in plain language: what it is for, how its users move through it, who those users are and what they may see and change, and the assumptions, constraints, limitations and dependencies that bound it. Section 3.2 turns this description into numbered requirements, and Section 3.3 shows how the platform is designed to meet them.

RescueVision is a proposed platform that gives Government, Police, Emergency Medical Services (EMS) and Fire agencies one shared picture of a disaster. It brings together damage seen in drone and satellite imagery, people who may need help, hazards such as floodwater near live power lines, and the state of roads, so that the agencies can decide where to send teams and how to reach them safely. The platform is designed to support people, not to replace them: every result produced by a model stays a candidate until a person reviews it.

Figure 3-1 shows the intended workflow. A Commander of the lead agency opens one shared incident and invites the other agencies. An Analyst brings in imagery, which is analysed in the background. The results appear on one map in 2D and, where suitable data exist, in 3D, each labelled with its source, its age and whether a person has reviewed it. Analysts confirm or correct what the models found. Commanders then open assistance cases and missions, assign teams and plan routes, while compound hazard alerts close roads that have become dangerous. Field Responders act on the ground and send updates, which return to the shared map. Verified citizen requests join the same list of cases, and approved reports carry the results to partner agencies.

The web command console is intended to be a single-page browser application built with React and Vite, for desktop browsers. The mobile field application is intended to be built with Expo (React Native) for Android and iOS, with offline storage on the device so that tasks and reports can be kept while the network is down. Both use one map engine, MapLibre GL, for the 2D map; the 3D view draws building shapes and precomputed 3D tiles produced from drone imagery with OpenDroneMap. The citizen channel is a short mobile form.

All three surfaces call one application interface built with FastAPI, which sends live changes to connected clients. Records are stored in PostgreSQL 18 with PostGIS 3.6 for geometry, pgRouting for route planning on the road network and pgvector for image embeddings. Row-level security in the database limits each agency to the incidents it has joined. Coordinates are stored in WGS 84, and distances are computed in metres. Large files are kept in S3-compatible object storage, and push-notification and SMS services deliver messages. The AI models run as separate services behind a job queue. For the Project II demonstration they are planned to run with ONNX Runtime on a single CPU server; the graphics processors in the deployment view of Section 3.3 describe the proposed configuration for an operational deployment.

3.2.1.3 Feature F1: Before/After Damage Assessment and Restoration Cost

After an earthquake, flood or storm, decision makers need two answers quickly: which buildings are damaged, and roughly what it will cost to restore them. F1 answers both at the level of a single building. Building footprints come from open map sources (OpenStreetMap or Overture), from AI extraction, or from manual entry. Where pre-event and post-event imagery both cover a building, the model compares them; where only post-event imagery exists, it assesses the post-event image alone and the result is labelled accordingly so users can weigh it.

Each assessed building receives one of the four grades of the xBD damage scale: No Damage, Minor Damage, Major Damage or Destroyed [2]. The model also reports a probability for each grade, so an Analyst can see the difference between a confident “Destroyed” and a borderline one. An Analyst or a field team may confirm or correct the grade. The platform keeps every assessment of a building as history and treats exactly one as current.

The indicative restoration cost follows the repair-ratio idea used in the FEMA Hazus methodology [31]. For a building with footprint area A and n floors, the floor area is A × n. The cost range is this floor area multiplied by the repair ratio for its damage grade and by the local unit cost per square metre for its occupancy and construction type. Both the ratio and the unit cost have a low and a high value, which gives a low–high range instead of a single figure that would suggest false precision. The unit costs and ratios live in editable cost profiles per region and currency. Once a cost estimate is published it is kept as a snapshot, so a report never changes silently when an assumption is later edited. The estimate supports planning and prioritisation; it is not an engineering survey or an insurance valuation.

3.2.1.4 Feature F2: 2D/3D Mapping and Rescue Route Planning

F2 gives every agency the same picture of the ground. The stitched orthomosaic is shown over a base map in 2D, and a 3D city view is built from the same drone imagery (surface and terrain models and a 3D mesh). Both views show the same layers: buildings, hazards, people, zones and routes. A user who selects a building in 2D still has it selected after switching to 3D.

Roads are held as a network of segments, each with a current condition: clear, debris, flooded, blocked or closed by a hazard. A condition may come from AI analysis, from a responder on the ground or from a verified citizen report, and the source is kept. Route planning then works for a specific vehicle. A four-wheel-drive rescue truck may cross shallow water that an ambulance must avoid, so each vehicle carries a maximum safe water depth. The planner uses shortest-path search [49] on the road network [52]. Closed segments, and flooded segments deeper than the vehicle can cross, are excluded. It returns a primary route and alternatives. When a road on an active route later closes, the route is marked invalid and the team is offered a new one. 3.2.1.5 Feature F3: Aerial Person Detection under Partial Visibility

Seen from a drone, people look very different from the upright figures in everyday photographs. They are small, viewed from above or at an angle, and in a disaster they are often partly hidden by debris, water, vegetation or a roof edge. Public aerial benchmarks such as VisDrone [42] and search-and-rescue studies such as HERIDAL [40] show how much harder detection becomes under these conditions. F3 is specified for this setting. A detection is required even when only a head or limbs are visible. The result says how much of the person was visible: full, partial, head only or limbs only, with an estimated occlusion ratio and, where the image allows, a posture.

A detection is useful to a rescue team only if it can be found on the ground. The platform therefore converts each image position into a map position and attaches an uncertainty radius in metres. The radius grows with coarser ground resolution and weaker GPS accuracy. Images taken from too high to resolve a person are not analysed, and the Analyst is told why. Thermal images are processed when the drone supplies them. Two limits of scope are stated explicitly. F3 covers people who are at least partly visible from the air, not people buried under rubble. Every detection is a candidate for a human to review, not a confirmed person.

3.2.1.6 Feature F4: Multi-Object Person Tracking and Assistance Cases

F4 turns isolated sightings into information a commander can act on, in three levels. A detection is one sighting in one image. A track links detections of the same person across consecutive frames or overlapping images and gives that person a stable identifier, in the manner of modern multi-object trackers such as ByteTrack [43]. An assistance case is a person, or a group, that a human has decided needs help. Each track keeps its path, last known position, time last seen and a movement state of moving or stationary. A person who stays still while the area around them changes may be injured or trapped, so stationary tracks are brought forward for review.

Assistance cases do not come from the drone alone. A verified citizen request or a responder’s report creates a case in the same list, so a commander works from one queue whatever the source. Cases are triaged with the four START categories, Immediate (red), Delayed (yellow), Minor (green) and Expectant (black) [66]. A case moves from detection to rescue, can be linked to the building where people may be trapped and to the hospital or shelter receiving them, and keeps a timestamped event history. Because a track describes the past, the platform always shows how old its last position is.

3.2.1.7 Feature F5: Compound Hazard Alerts (“Electrified Water”)

Disasters rarely produce one danger at a time. Floodwater is dangerous, and so is a fallen power line. A street flooded next to a line that is still energised can kill a responder who wades through it, even though neither hazard alone would have stopped the team. F5 watches for such combinations. The platform keeps two kinds of record: hazards (such as flood, fire, gas leak, structural collapse, smoke, downed power line, debris, sinkhole and chemical spill), reported by AI, responders or citizens; and infrastructure assets (power lines, transformers and gas pipelines) with a power state that the utility or an authorised user keeps current.

A rule engine compares the two. Its first rule is named Electrified Water. It fires when an active flood hazard lies within the configured rule distance of a power line or transformer that has not been confirmed de-energised. The rule and buffer distances require confirmation with civil-defence and utility guidance before operational use. When the rule fires, the platform does four things in one step. It draws a buffered danger zone and shows it as a no-entry zone. It closes every road segment inside that zone. It marks active routes through those roads as invalid and offers new ones. It warns the assigned teams and every responder whose last position is in or near the zone. An asset whose power state is unknown is treated as energised. When the utility confirms the line is off and a Commander resolves the alert, the roads it closed reopen, unless another active alert still closes them. Rules are stored as data, so further combinations, such as a gas leak near a fire, can be added later without changing the program.

This section describes what RescueVision presents to its users and what it exchanges with equipment and outside services. It stays at the descriptive level; screen illustrations are given in Section 3.3.

RescueVision has three user-facing surfaces. The web command console serves Commanders, Analysts and administrators. It is built around the map, with a layer panel, an alert banner, case and mission lists, and a report workspace. The mobile field application serves field responders. It needs large touch targets, high contrast for outdoor use, a one-touch SOS control and a clear indicator when the device is offline. The citizen channel is a short mobile form for requesting help. On every surface, the interface must show uncertainty openly: what the AI estimated, how confident it was, whether a person has reviewed it, and how old the information is.

The platform does not control drones. It receives what they capture. RescueVision relies on a small number of external services: object storage for image files; open base-map and building-footprint data; the AI inference service that runs the detection, damage and tracking models; a power-state feed from the utility where one can be agreed; push-notification services for the mobile application; and an SMS gateway for citizen one-time codes. The nonfunctional requirements set the quality the platform must reach. In emergency work, some of these matter as much as the features: a warning that arrives late or a position shown as current when it is ten minutes old can mislead a team. The numbers are proposed targets for a future evaluation. They are not measured results, and they remain open for agreement with the supervisor.
The 2D map shall display the incident layers within 3 s for an area of up to 25 km² on a 20 Mbit/s connection.
A responder position shall appear on the command map within 10 s of being sent.
A route over a road network of up to 50,000 segments shall be computed within 5 s.
An Electrified Water alert shall be raised, and its notifications sent, within 60 s of the triggering hazard or asset change being recorded.
An analysis job shall report its progress at least every 30 s.

The platform shall serve at least 200 concurrent users across all agencies of one incident, each viewing the map and sending updates (proposed workload; to be confirmed), while meeting NFR-PF-01 to NFR-PF-04.
The platform shall be available at least 99.5% of the time while an incident is active.
No upload, report or status change acknowledged to a user shall be lost after the failure of a single application server or analysis worker.
Interrupted image uploads shall resume without restarting the whole session.
Map viewing, case management and route planning shall remain available when the AI inference service is unavailable.
Data shall be backed up daily, and a restore shall be tested before the platform is used in an exercise.
No AI result shall by itself confirm a person, close a case or dispatch a team; these actions shall require a user.
Where information is missing, safety-related defaults shall favour caution, for example by treating an unknown power state as energised.
Road closures made automatically by an alert shall be reversible only through resolving that alert, by a Commander.
Cost estimates shall carry a notice that they are indicative and are not engineering or insurance valuations.
Passwords and session refresh tokens shall never be stored in readable form.
Every request shall be checked against the user’s role permissions and the agency’s incident participation.
Administrators and Commanders shall use multi-factor authentication.
Web sessions shall expire after 30 minutes of inactivity.

It covers the System Analysis and Design topics listed in the Project I guide [4]: architecture, design rationale, database and file design, user interface design, class, sequence and use case diagrams, and the detailed design of the parts that carry the most risk. Two sources of notation are used throughout. Structural and behavioural diagrams follow the Unified Modeling Language (UML) 2.5.1 [69]. Two choices about volume complete the physical design. Every geometry column has a spatial index, and the two tables that grow fastest, responder positions and the audit log, are divided into monthly partitions. Old months can then be archived or deleted as whole units when the retention period ends (NFR-PV-04), without slowing the current month.

Decision D-04 places access control in the database. The design uses PostgreSQL row-level security [71]: every one of the 56 tables has security enabled and denies access by default, and policies then open exactly the rows each kind of user may see. Applications never connect as the owner of the schema. Instead, each connects through one of the four group roles in Table 3-43.
Table 3-43: Database roles and what they may access
The application interface, acting for a signed-in agency user.
Rows allowed by the policies for that user's agency, role and incident participation.
All operational rows; it acts for the platform, not for a user.
Only the citizen's own profile, requests and photos.
Read-only operational data; no credentials, sessions, citizen identities or audit log.

At the start of each request, the application interface records the identifier of the signed-in user for the duration of that transaction only, so a pooled connection cannot carry one user's identity into another user's request. Every policy derives the user's agency, role and permissions from that identifier at the time of the request. A suspended user therefore loses access on the next request, and an agency loses access to an incident as soon as its participation is withdrawn (FR-AC-05, NFR-PV-02). Draft reports remain visible only inside the authoring agency until they are approved or shared (FR-RP-04, FR-RP-06).

Policies decide which rows a user may change; column guards decide which fields. A field responder may change the status of a mission they are assigned to but not its target or priority, and users may edit their own name and phone number but not their role or agency. Password hashes cannot be read by any application role; sign-in uses a single protected function. Inserts, updates and deletes on 27 operational tables are written to the audit log with the acting user and the values before and after the change (NFR-SC-05), and no application role can modify the log (NFR-SC-06). The design will be reviewed against the OWASP Application Security Verification Standard before any field trial, as NFR-SC-07 requires [67].

Large binary files do not belong in database rows. Images, raster products, citizen photos and report PDFs are kept in object storage, and the database stores a storage key and a SHA-256 checksum for each file (IR-SW-01). The demonstration uses a single urban crop and two dates separated by about seven months. Differences in lighting, viewing geometry, image alignment, intervening land use, and post-event activity can influence the pixel-change layer. The report should record the evaluation split, class definitions, and metrics before drawing conclusions about accuracy. The team can then test how the map distinguishes model predictions, reported hazards, and confirmed conditions.

Later prototypes should document evidence for 3D views, authorized assistance records, and route guidance based on verified road information. These steps inform the Project II work discussed in Chapter 5.

This chapter discusses how far Project I meets the objectives set in Chapter 1, states the limitations of the work, draws conclusions and sets out the work planned for Project II. It separates what the report specifies and designs from what the evidence so far shows.

Project I set six objectives (Table 1-2). For each one, the report now contains requirements in Section 3.2, linked in Table 3-38, and design elements in Section 3.3, linked in Table 3-48. Prototype evidence in Chapter 4 covers only part of the first two objectives. The discussion below takes each objective in turn.
OBJ-01, a consistent spatial view in 2D and 3D.

The requirements specify one georeferenced map with the same layers in 2D and 3D and a selection that survives switching between them (FR-MR-01 to FR-MR-05). Section 3.3 places the map at the centre of the console and stores all geometry in one coordinate system. The prototype in Chapter 4 shows two dated satellite images of the same area in one 2D frame and a synchronised side-by-side view; it does not show a base map, an orthomosaic or a 3D view. The objective is therefore specified and designed, and partly demonstrated in 2D.
OBJ-02, damage and indicative cost linked to their evidence.

The requirements specify four damage grades with their probabilities, a label for the assessment method, review by an Analyst and a low–high cost range with visible assumptions (FR-DC-01 to FR-DC-13). Every AI result keeps its model version and input images (FR-IM-07), which answers the provenance gap identified in Chapter 2. The prototype shows a pixel-change layer over a dated image pair, but no damage grades, confidence values or costs. No model has yet been trained or evaluated on project data.
OBJ-03, people who may need help and hazards, including compound hazards.

The requirements treat every aerial detection as a candidate with a position uncertainty in metres (FR-PD-01 to FR-PD-10), follow people across images into tracks and assistance cases (FR-PT-01 to FR-PT-12) and specify the Electrified Water rule, which treats an unknown power state as energised (FR-HZ-01 to FR-HZ-13). Section 3.3 gives the case and alert life cycles and the rule evaluation. Chapter 2 found that compound hazards are recognised in hazard research but not acted on by the systems reviewed; RescueVision addresses this in its design, but no part of OBJ-03 has yet been demonstrated.

The requirements and design centre on one shared incident that a lead agency opens and others join, with common roles across agencies, missions per agency and reports that a Commander approves before they are shared (FR-AC-01 to FR-AC-11, FR-RP-01 to FR-RP-11). Database row-level security is designed to keep each agency to the incidents it has joined. This responds to the coordination obstacles reported in the literature, but whether it improves coordination can only be shown with users.

Routing is specified per vehicle, excluding closed segments and floodwater deeper than the vehicle can cross, with an explicit no-route result and re-planning when a road closes (FR-MR-06 to FR-MR-13). The design uses graph search on the road network inside the database. The prototype’s route symbols are placeholders, so no route has yet been computed.
OBJ-06, visible uncertainty and enforced permissions.

Requirements on confidence, review state, data age and permissions (IR-UI-05, IR-UI-06, NFR-DQ-01, NFR-DQ-03, NFR-SC-02) are reflected in the design’s review states and access rules. They are untested.

Taken together, Project I delivers a consistent specification and design for all six objectives, with requirement and design identifiers linked from objective to diagram, and preliminary visual evidence for two of them. The proposal responds to each of the four gaps identified in Section 2.9: a design for transfer testing, provenance and visible uncertainty, joined people-finding channels and compound hazard alerts. None of these responses has yet been tested.
No model has been trained or evaluated on project data, and no performance target in Section 3.2.4 has been measured. Every number in the requirements is a proposal.

The prototype covers one urban area of about 0.8 × 0.8 km and two acquisition dates. Its change layer is a pixel-difference illustration whose method is not yet documented in the repository, so it supports no damage claim.
The public datasets cover a few events and regions, and models trained on them may perform worse on local buildings. Map position depends on GPS and ground control, and may be wrong by metres.
Human review of every AI result.

The design relies on Analysts to review detections, grades and tracks. In a large incident the review workload could delay decisions; the design ranks stationary tracks and alerts first, but this has not been tested.

Detections, tracks and citizen requests describe vulnerable people. The design limits access to participating agencies and sets retention rules, but the retention period and legal basis still have to be agreed.
Treating an unknown power state as energised is safe but may close passable roads until the utility confirms a line is off.
No emergency-service user has yet tested the interface or the workflow.

Responding agencies need to know quickly which buildings are damaged, where people may need help, which hazards make roads dangerous and how to reach those people, and they need to share that picture with each other. Chapter 2 showed that research and operational systems address these needs separately, rarely show how uncertain each output is and do not act on combined hazards such as floodwater near live power lines.

Project I responds with a specification and design for RescueVision. The report defines six objectives and six features, 167 uniquely identified requirements and ten use cases, and a design that links each requirement to its architecture, data and interface elements. The design keeps one shared incident for all agencies, treats every AI result as a candidate until a person confirms it, keeps the provenance of every result and raises compound hazard alerts that close roads and re-plan routes.

The evidence so far is limited. A preliminary prototype shows two dated satellite images of one area in a common 2D frame and a change layer for inspection. It does not show damage grades, people, hazards or routes, and no accuracy or speed has been measured. The report therefore establishes what RescueVision is designed to do and how it is designed to do it; it does not yet show that the platform works or that it improves a response.
Project II is planned to turn the design into a working platform and to test it. The planned work is:

Train the damage, building, flood and person-detection models on xBD, FloodNet, RescueNet and SARD, and report per-class results on held-out disaster events using the metrics set in Section 3.2.4. Compare the configured EfficientNet-B3 classifier with one agreed DINO backbone on the same building crops.
Load a road network from OpenStreetMap or Overture, compute vehicle-specific routes with closures and flood depths, and measure how often a blocked road is wrongly marked safe.
Produce 3D tiles from drone imagery with OpenDroneMap and measure their position error against ground control points.
Link detections into tracks, convert confirmed tracks into assistance cases and connect verified citizen requests to the same case list.
Implement the Electrified Water rule with its road closures and re-planning, and confirm the rule distances with civil-defence or utility advice.
Complete the mobile field application with offline storage and SOS, and run a task-based evaluation of the console and the mobile application with emergency-service users or a tabletop exercise.

A SWOT analysis sets out the internal strengths and weaknesses of the proposed platform next to the external opportunities and threats in the environment where it would be used. Strengths and weaknesses describe RescueVision itself: its features, data and design choices. Opportunities and threats describe things the team does not control, such as regulation, partner agencies, networks and public expectations. The main strength of RescueVision is that it brings work that is usually spread across separate tools into one shared incident. Government, Police, EMS and Fire teams see the same map, the same people who may need help and the same hazards. Every AI result is specified to keep a link to the model version and the images that produced it (FR-IM-07), so a Commander can check where a number came from before acting on it. The platform also joins features that support one another. Building-damage information helps prioritise locations for review. Verified assistance cases can become route destinations, and confirmed hazards can restrict road access. Person detection is specified for partly visible people and always reports a position uncertainty in metres. Routing is specified to take into account the vehicle and the depth of floodwater. Hazard rules and cost profiles are stored as data, so they can be adapted to a new region without rewriting the program. Finally, the intended open-source geospatial stack carries no licence fees, although hosting, support and staff time still have to be paid for.

The quality of every AI layer depends on its training data. Public disaster imagery datasets exist, such as xBD for satellite imagery [2] and FloodNet and RescueNet for drone imagery [25], [26], but they cover a limited range of building styles, regions and image conditions. The models may therefore perform worse on local buildings than published results suggest. Aerial imagery cannot show people under rubble or inside buildings; the platform states this limit rather than hiding it. Cost estimates are only as good as the local unit costs entered in the cost profiles, and those figures still have to be collected. The platform needs drones, flying weather and some network connection to work at full capacity. Its analysis is also computationally heavy. Stitching an orthomosaic, building a 3D model and running detection, damage and tracking models over hundreds of high-resolution images need powerful graphics processors (GPUs) and large memory. Without that hardware, or affordable cloud capacity, results arrive more slowly, just when speed matters most. The Electrified Water rule depends on knowing whether a line is energised, which requires cooperation from the utility. Lastly, the platform is a proposal. It has not yet been evaluated with real response agencies.

Drones are increasingly studied for surveying disaster areas and supporting response [34], which creates a place for a platform that turns their images into decisions. Open map data (OpenStreetMap, Overture) and open datasets and models lower the cost of building and testing such a platform. International disaster-risk policy keeps the understanding of disaster risk and preparedness for response among its priorities [1]. There is room to partner with civil defence for realistic scenarios, with universities for annotated data, and with utilities for power-state information. Because hazard rules are data, new combinations such as a gas leak near a fire can be added later. Historical incidents stored in the platform could also support training exercises and post-event learning.

Drone flights need permits and are limited by airspace rules, which may delay or prevent imaging at the moment it is most needed. Aerial images of people raise privacy and legal questions, and public trust could suffer if the data were misused. There is also a risk that users trust the AI too much: a missed person or a false alarm in a rescue setting has real consequences. Networks are often damaged in a disaster area. Agencies may be reluctant to share data with each other or to change established ways of working. As a public-safety system, the platform would also be an attractive target for cyber attacks.
